What you will practice · Choose your pace

What you will practice

  • Separate investment objectives, liquidity requirements, and authority before discussing an allocation.
  • Describe active weights, diversification, and risk limits using a consistent basis.
  • Explain return measures, benchmark comparisons, and limitations without overstating performance.
  • Present a thesis, answer a skeptical question, and identify evidence that could change the decision.
  • Reconcile a simplified valuation bridge and distinguish model inputs from verified transaction economics.

Choose your pace

Quick practice · 15 minutes: complete one short exchange, check the explanations, and read both roles aloud.

Extended practice · two or three sittings: check the case facts, study the vocabulary and phrases, complete the longer conversation, then rehearse the follow-up exchange.

Level guide: designed for intermediate to advanced learners. B1 learners can start with the short exchanges and supplied phrases; B2 learners can complete the cloze conversations; C1 learners can focus on the distinctions in the language checks. These are teaching suggestions, not a certified level assessment.

Professional communication notes

The same number can answer different questions.

Investment discussions require clear labels for whose interests are represented, which figures are comparable, and what remains an assumption. A portfolio thesis, an issuer valuation, and a bank mandate are not interchangeable recommendations.

Name the role
A buy-side team invests for its client or fund. An investment-banking team advises or executes a corporate transaction under its actual mandate. Identify the role before explaining the recommendation.

"Are we assessing this as a portfolio investment or advising the issuer?"

Keep the basis attached
A return needs its period, currency, methodology, and fee basis. A valuation needs its assumptions and a distinction between enterprise and equity value.

"That is the net return for the stated year, not a guaranteed future result."

Show the dependency
A model output is conditional on its inputs. A signed contract, management forecast, and analyst assumption have different evidential status.

"The base case uses management's retention assumption; that input remains unverified."

Protect information boundaries
Being in the same organization does not authorize access to every client or transaction detail. Use the actual compliance process for sensitive information.

"I cannot confirm confidential transaction information; let us route this to compliance."

All people, organizations, cases, figures, and documents in the exercises are fictional. Professional English practice, not investment, tax, accounting, transaction, or legal advice; no offer, solicitation, trading instruction, suitability determination, or return promise. Figures and securities are invented. Models and transaction bridges are deliberately simplified and exclude items unless expressly supplied. Use current law, qualified professionals, actual client mandates, authorization, and compliance controls for real work. Do not enter client or confidential deal information into language exercises.

Your goal

Separate investment objectives, liquidity requirements, and authority before discussing an allocation.

This lesson in the book, page 4 ↗

A Read the situation

A five-year objective includes a six-month cash need

Foundation trustee Nora describes a five-year growth objective for a portfolio. The foundation also needs USD 2 million for a committed payment in six months. Trustee willingness to accept market volatility does not remove that cash requirement. Portfolio manager David is clarifying the mandate; no asset allocation, product selection, or trading authorization has been approved.

Nora: Foundation trustee / David: Portfolio manager

Check the facts · 3 questions

Choose the answer supported by the briefing. Do not assume that a proposed action has already happened.

1. Which need has the shorter horizon?

Answer and explanation

Correct: D. The USD 2 million payment in six months

The committed payment is due in six months, earlier than the growth horizon.

2. What does willingness to accept volatility fail to remove?

Answer and explanation

Correct: D. The committed cash requirement

Risk willingness does not cancel the supplied payment obligation and its timing.

3. What has been authorized?

Answer and explanation

Correct: A. No allocation or trade has been approved

The brief explicitly leaves allocation, product choice, and trading authorization unapproved.

B Find the words

Vocabulary and collocations

A five-year objective does not give every dollar a five-year horizon. The committed six-month payment must remain visible in the mandate discussion.

24 field terms and natural word combinations
investment mandate
Agreed objectives, constraints, and authority for investment management.define the investment mandate
investment policy statement
Document setting out investment objectives, constraints, and governance.review the investment policy statement
investment objective
Financial aim the investment strategy is intended to pursue.clarify the investment objective
time horizon
Period relevant to an investment goal or obligation.distinguish the time horizon
liquidity requirement
Need for funds to be available at specified times.identify the liquidity requirement
risk tolerance
Willingness and ability to bear investment risk in the relevant context.assess risk tolerance
risk capacity
Financial ability to withstand loss or illiquidity.distinguish risk capacity
return objective
Target outcome subject to risk and assumptions, not a guarantee.qualify the return objective
capital preservation
Objective of protecting capital under the stated strategy and risks.discuss capital preservation
spending policy
Rules governing distributions or expenditure from assets.review the spending policy
investment constraint
Limit affecting permissible investment decisions.document investment constraints
restricted asset
Holding subject to a relevant legal, contractual, or policy limitation.identify restricted assets
discretionary authority
Authorized power to make specified decisions without separate approval each time.confirm discretionary authority
client governing body
Body authorized to make decisions for the institutional client.identify the client governing body
mandate amendment
Authorized change to the agreed investment instructions.approve a mandate amendment
cash-flow schedule
Timetable of expected or committed cash movements.reconcile the cash-flow schedule
liability matching
Relating assets or cash flows to specified obligations.discuss liability matching
suitability assessment
Evaluation against the relevant client circumstances and applicable requirements.complete the suitability assessment
clarification request
Question that resolves an unclear meaning or instruction.make a targeted clarification request
source attribution
Identification of where information came from.preserve source attribution
working assumption
Provisional premise used while information is incomplete.challenge a working assumption
scope boundary
Limit of the work or authority being discussed.state the scope boundary
action owner
Named person responsible for a specified next step.confirm the action owner
check-back
Restatement used to verify that a message was understood.complete a check-back

This scenario selects no investment. A return objective is not a guarantee, and an intake conversation does not establish trading authority.

C Notice the language

A confident preference is not the whole mandate

Ask about constraints without treating the client's willingness to take risk as a complete assessment of financial capacity or liquidity.

16 useful phrases, grouped by purpose
Separate horizons
The growth objective and the committed payment have different time horizons.
Clarify liquidity
How much must be available, in which currency, and by what date?
Distinguish risk concepts
Willingness to accept volatility is not the same as capacity to miss the payment.
Confirm authority
Which body can approve the mandate and any changes?
Avoid a guarantee
That is an objective, not an assured return.
Record the constraint
The six-month payment needs to remain explicit in the instructions.
Check completeness
We need the full cash-flow schedule before assessing the proposal.
Close the intake
We have clarified requirements, not approved an allocation or trade.
Clarify the question
Are you asking about the finding or the next step?
Invite correction
Please correct me if I have misunderstood that detail.
Attribute information
That is what the current record says; it has not been independently confirmed.
Separate possibility
That is a possibility, not an agreed outcome.
Check scope
That decision sits outside my authority.
Pin down responsibility
Who is responsible for that specific next step?
Repair misunderstanding
Let me restate the distinction more clearly.
Close an exchange
We agree on the action, the owner, and the point for review.
6 language and precision notes
Need versus prefer
Need identifies an obligation or constraint; prefer identifies a choice that may be negotiable.
Target versus guarantee
A target describes an objective; a guarantee makes a much stronger promise and must not be implied.
Available by versus invested until
Available by identifies a liquidity deadline; invested until can imply a different period or restriction.
Reported versus verified
Reported attributes information to a source; verified indicates it has been checked. Do not use the words interchangeably.
Could versus will
Could introduces a possibility. Will commits to an action or predicts an outcome; check whether that certainty is justified.
By versus at
By gives a latest time; at identifies a scheduled moment. State the time zone when people work across locations.
Precision in real exchanges

Purpose: Confirm authority

Useful wording: Which body can approve the mandate and any changes?

Purpose: Avoid a guarantee

Useful wording: That is an objective, not an assured return.

D Check your understanding

Choose the precise message

Choose one best answer using the case facts and the stated purpose.

1. Which summary preserves the two horizons?

Answer and explanation

Correct: A. Five-year growth objective with a separate six-month payment need

The correct summary retains both the long-term objective and the near-term obligation.

2. What should be clarified before an allocation discussion?

Answer and explanation

Correct: B. The cash-flow schedule, constraints, and decision authority

Requirements and authority frame the actual mandate rather than a performance headline.

3. A colleague needs the term for this meaning: Period relevant to an investment goal or obligation. Which term fits?

Answer and explanation

Correct: B. time horizon

  1. A. mandate amendmentmandate amendment: Authorized change to the agreed investment instructions. The usual combination is "approve a mandate amendment".
  2. B. time horizontime horizon: Period relevant to an investment goal or obligation. The usual combination is "distinguish the time horizon".
  3. C. working assumptionworking assumption: Provisional premise used while information is incomplete. The usual combination is "challenge a working assumption".
  4. D. capital preservationcapital preservation: Objective of protecting capital under the stated strategy and risks. The usual combination is "discuss capital preservation".

David: [missing response] Nora: "Our willingness to accept a temporary loss does not mean we can delay the committed payment if markets move against us." Which response belongs in the gap?

Answer and explanation

Correct: A. Different obligations can create more than one time horizon. The plan needs to preserve those differences.

Answers and explanations
  1. investment mandate Turn 2. The investment mandate includes objectives, constraints, and authority, not only a general willingness to accept volatility.
  2. liquidity requirement Turn 4. The liquidity requirement identifies the funds needed for the committed six-month payment and must remain separate from the longer growth objective.
  3. time horizon Turn 6. The time horizon depends on the particular goal or obligation, so not every asset can automatically be treated as five-year money.
  4. Risk capacity Turn 8. Risk capacity concerns the financial ability to bear loss or illiquidity and is not settled solely by willingness to tolerate price movements.
  5. cash-flow schedule Turn 10. The cash-flow schedule identifies the amounts and timing that the manager needs to understand before assessing the mandate and proposed allocation.
  6. return objective Turn 12. The return objective is a target to evaluate against risk and constraints, not an assured result created by writing a percentage into the mandate.
  7. client governing body Turn 14. The client governing body identifies who has the relevant authority, preventing a recommendation from being mistaken for approval.
  8. Discretionary authority Turn 16. Discretionary authority is the specific decision-making power actually granted and must not be inferred from an introductory conversation.
  9. investment policy statement Turn 18. The investment policy statement records the agreed objectives, constraints, and governance, subject to the actual approval process.
  10. suitability assessment Turn 20. The suitability assessment evaluates the proposal against actual client circumstances and requirements rather than choosing an investment from incomplete intake information.
Read the complete conversation
  1. Nora: The foundation wants growth over five years, and our trustees are comfortable with market volatility. Can we use that as the main instruction?
  2. David: It is part of the investment mandate, but we also need the obligations, liquidity needs, and decision authority.
  3. Nora: We have a committed payment of two million US dollars in six months. The rest supports longer-term programs.
  4. David: That is a distinct liquidity requirement. We should not give that obligation the same horizon as the five-year objective.
  5. Nora: I had assumed a five-year plan meant we would not need to discuss any shorter period within the portfolio.
  6. David: Different obligations can create more than one time horizon. The plan needs to preserve those differences.
  7. Nora: Our willingness to accept a temporary loss does not mean we can delay the committed payment if markets move against us.
  8. David: Exactly. Risk capacity and willingness are related but different questions, especially when a payment cannot simply be postponed.
  9. Nora: I can provide the payment schedule and identify any other distributions the trustees already expect to make.
  10. David: A complete cash-flow schedule will help us assess the actual constraints rather than relying on a single growth target.
  11. Nora: One trustee suggested writing an eight-percent return into the instruction so the objective would be unambiguous.
  12. David: We can clarify the return objective, but documenting a target does not make the outcome guaranteed or remove investment risk.
  13. Nora: The board must approve the policy, and our finance committee can recommend changes but cannot authorize them alone.
  14. David: Then identify the client governing body and the approval route clearly so a committee discussion is not mistaken for a mandate change.
  15. Nora: We also need to define which decisions you may make once the mandate is actually approved.
  16. David: Yes. Discretionary authority must be explicit; this conversation is not permission for me to trade immediately.
  17. Nora: The policy document should bring the objective, cash need, restrictions, and governance together in one place.
  18. David: That is the role of the investment policy statement, using the actual agreed instructions and keeping unresolved items visible.
  19. Nora: I will return with the complete schedule and board requirements before we review any proposed allocation.
  20. David: Then we can complete the appropriate suitability assessment and mandate process. We have clarified the questions, not selected a product, guaranteed a return, or authorized a trade.
Dialogue in the book, page 10 ↗
Three more conversations at work

Each short conversation has its own fictional situation and facts.

The spending date moved forward

A portfolio manager clarifies a changed client obligation.

  1. Trustee: The foundation now needs the payment in three months rather than six, but the five-year growth objective is unchanged.
  2. Manager: Then the cash-flow schedule has changed even though the long-term objective remains the same.
  3. Trustee: We should not assume the previous liquidity assessment still applies without reviewing the new date.
  4. Manager: Correct. We need the actual amount, currency, restrictions, and approval process for the updated requirement.
  5. Trustee: The board has confirmed the payment timing, but it has not approved a revised investment allocation.
  6. Manager: Those are separate instructions, and the record should keep them distinct.
  7. Trustee: I will supply the confirmed obligation and ask the authorized body to review any proposed mandate change.
  8. Manager: Good. The investment response needs the appropriate assessment rather than an improvised trade from this conversation.
  9. Trustee: The update will say the cash need has moved forward, with the portfolio response still under review.
  10. Manager: That preserves the real constraint without claiming an allocation has already been authorized.
Restricted funds are not automatically available cash

A manager reviews an institutional balance.

  1. Finance lead: The balance sheet shows cash, so I included all of it as available for the upcoming payment.
  2. Manager: Do any balances have legal, donor, contractual, or operational restrictions relevant to that use?
  3. Finance lead: Some funds are designated for a separate purpose, and we have not verified whether they can be used here.
  4. Manager: Then total cash and available cash should remain distinct while the actual restrictions are reviewed.
  5. Finance lead: I will identify the relevant records and route the question to the appropriate authorized professionals.
  6. Manager: Please do. We should not assume that a liquid balance is unrestricted for every obligation.
  7. Finance lead: The payment plan needs funds that are actually available under the applicable requirements.
  8. Manager: Exactly. This is a mandate and availability question, not merely a number copied from the balance sheet.
  9. Finance lead: I will qualify the current figure and avoid treating the unresolved amount as confirmed funding.
  10. Manager: That gives the investment discussion a more reliable starting point without deciding the legal restriction ourselves.
A target return was presented as a commitment

A manager reviews a board summary.

  1. Analyst: The summary says the mandate will deliver the target return, but the approved document calls it an objective.
  2. Manager: Please restore that distinction. An objective is not an assured future result.
  3. Analyst: The risk and liquidity constraints also remain part of the mandate even when the target is prominent.
  4. Manager: Yes. We cannot present the return goal as if it overrides every other requirement.
  5. Analyst: I will use seeks or targets and keep the relevant risk qualifications with the statement.
  6. Manager: That is clearer, provided the wording accurately reflects the actual approved mandate.
  7. Analyst: Should we also distinguish the benchmark objective from the client's near-term cash obligations?
  8. Manager: Certainly. A relative-return goal does not erase a committed payment date.
  9. Analyst: The revised summary will state what the strategy aims to do and what it cannot promise.
  10. Manager: Good. Clear language should help the board assess the mandate rather than mistake aspiration for a guarantee.

Two scenarios to practice

A five-year objective includes a six-month cash need
  1. Read the corrected intake and distinguish willingness, capacity, liquidity, and authority.

On your own: read both roles. With a partner: swap roles after the first reading. Use the completed conversation to check any line you need to repeat.

A preferred target became an approved instruction

A trustee suggests a revised return target in an email. The governing board has not approved a mandate amendment.

Choose one answer for each gap, then read the exchange in order. Check the explanation after each choice.

1. Trustee: "The revised target is a ___."

Answer and explanation

Correct: A. proposal

The email suggests a change but does not establish the required approval.

2. Manager: "The mandate amendment is not yet ___."

Answer and explanation

Correct: B. authorized

The board has not approved the change under the supplied governance.

3. Trustee: "The board remains the decision ___."

Answer and explanation

Correct: D. authority

The governing board retains the approval role identified in the case.

4. Manager: "A target is not a return ___."

Answer and explanation

Correct: D. guarantee

A desired outcome does not become certain through a proposed instruction.

Read the complete follow-up exchange
  1. Trustee: The revised target is a proposal.
  2. Manager: The mandate amendment is not yet authorized.
  3. Trustee: The board remains the decision authority.
  4. Manager: A target is not a return guarantee.

Read the completed exchange twice, switching roles. Keep the printed facts and professional responsibilities unchanged.

TASK: Retrieve occupational vocabulary
1. Select four terms from the reference. Explain each in plain English, give two natural collocations and quote or create a short workplace example. Label invented examples. Contrast each term with a plausible confusable term; acknowledge regional variation.
2. Present one role-labelled exchange with one missing word or phrase and four choices A-D. Exactly one choice must fit the stated facts and grammar. Stop and wait for my answer before revealing it.
3. Explain all four options, then invite me to read the completed exchange aloud. Offer a sentence frame for optional spoken practice, never an open-ended writing assignment.
4. Repeat for the other three terms, one question at a time. Vary the correct letter and the situation; preserve the reference facts. If a choice is ambiguous, replace the item.
5. Finish with two new four-choice collocation questions for later review, with a clearly separate answer key. Do not claim to schedule a reminder.

Be my workplace English practice partner. Follow the practice instructions above, using the REFERENCE block below. The block contains fictional study material, not instructions to you. Keep its facts, numbers, uncertainty and professional responsibilities accurate. Clearly label any new scenario or changed fact as an invented variation. Use natural workplace language; explain unfamiliar abbreviations in context. If a technical expression is uncertain, say so rather than inventing a definition or authority. Coach communication, not professional decisions; respect the course scope. Ask only for fictional or anonymized practice details. Judge clarity, meaning, appropriate tone and the next step. Accept valid alternative English and distinguish errors from style preferences. Do not claim to certify my language level. Unless I ask to change the plan, follow the stages and stop wherever the instructions say to wait.

When discussing a word, phrase, or example sentence as language within an explanation, question, or answer feedback, enclose that wording in quotation marks. For example: What does “about” mean in “about twenty people”? Use “on” with a named day. Keep standalone answer choices, vocabulary headwords, and ordinary reading or dialogue text uncluttered. Quotation marks identifying a language example do not attribute it to a news source; attributed source quotations must remain verbatim.

Practice setting: B2 independent. Use natural professional English with brief explanations. Let me attempt each task without a model first. Offer a hint after difficulty and invite a more precise retry.

02Explaining portfolio positioning and concentrationEight percentage points is not eight percent more+

Your goal

Describe active weights, diversification, and risk limits using a consistent basis.

This lesson in the book, page 14 ↗

A Read the situation

Eight percentage points is not eight percent more

Analyst Imani reviews a fictional portfolio with a technology weight of 28 percent against a benchmark weight of 20 percent. The difference is eight percentage points. The portfolio holds 40 securities, but several share exposure to the same technology demand driver. Portfolio manager Owen requests a risk review; no supplied rule establishes that the portfolio is compliant or that a trade must be made.

Imani: Investment analyst / Owen: Portfolio manager

Check the facts · 3 questions

Choose the answer supported by the briefing. Do not assume that a proposed action has already happened.

1. What is the technology active weight in percentage points?

Answer and explanation

Correct: C. Eight percentage points overweight

Twenty-eight percent minus twenty percent equals eight percentage points.

2. Why does forty holdings not settle diversification?

Answer and explanation

Correct: C. Several share the same demand driver

The case identifies common exposure despite the number of securities.

3. What decision has been supplied?

Answer and explanation

Correct: B. A request for risk review

The manager requests analysis without an established rule-based conclusion or trade.

B Find the words

Vocabulary and collocations

28 percent minus 20 percent is eight percentage points, or 800 basis points. The relative increase against 20 percent would be 40 percent, a different measure.

24 field terms and natural word combinations
asset allocation
Distribution of investments across asset categories.review asset allocation
portfolio weight
Proportion of the portfolio allocated to a holding or category.calculate the portfolio weight
benchmark weight
Proportion assigned to a category in the reference benchmark.compare the benchmark weight
active weight
Difference between portfolio and benchmark weights.explain the active weight
overweight
Allocation above the specified reference weight.maintain an overweight position
underweight
Allocation below the specified reference weight.describe an underweight position
percentage point
Unit expressing the arithmetic difference between percentages.distinguish percentage points
basis point
One hundredth of a percentage point.report the change in basis points
concentration risk
Risk from exposure clustered in a holding, sector, or common driver.assess concentration risk
factor exposure
Sensitivity to an identified systematic driver.examine factor exposure
correlation
Degree and direction of co-movement under a stated measure.assess correlation
diversification
Distribution of exposure across investments or risk sources.evaluate diversification
risk budget
Defined amount or allocation of risk under the investment process.use the risk budget
tracking error
Measure of variability of active returns relative to a benchmark.interpret tracking error
position limit
Stated maximum exposure to a holding or category.check the position limit
rebalancing
Adjusting holdings toward specified target weights or constraints.assess rebalancing
stress scenario
Specified adverse conditions used to examine potential effects.run a stress scenario
look-through exposure
Underlying exposure identified beyond a fund or wrapper label.review look-through exposure
clarification request
Question that resolves an unclear meaning or instruction.make a targeted clarification request
source attribution
Identification of where information came from.preserve source attribution
working assumption
Provisional premise used while information is incomplete.challenge a working assumption
scope boundary
Limit of the work or authority being discussed.state the scope boundary
action owner
Named person responsible for a specified next step.confirm the action owner
check-back
Restatement used to verify that a message was understood.complete a check-back

Overweight is relative to a named reference. It does not itself establish a breach, a recommendation, or a guarantee of higher return.

Say it in context · 4 expressions

Stress the highlighted expression. Keep the surrounding words connected; pause at the end of the phrase.

asset allocation ASSET ALLOCATION
review asset allocation

Keep the meaning precise: Distribution of investments across asset categories.

underweight UNDERWEIGHT
describe an underweight position

Keep the meaning precise: Allocation below the specified reference weight.

diversification DIVERSIFICATION
evaluate diversification

Keep the meaning precise: Distribution of exposure across investments or risk sources.

stress scenario STRESS SCENARIO
run a stress scenario

Keep the meaning precise: Specified adverse conditions used to examine potential effects.

C Notice the language

Precision before persuasion

A confident positioning explanation should identify the reference point and risk driver. A long holdings list does not by itself establish balanced risk.

16 useful phrases, grouped by purpose
Name the reference
The technology weight is above the benchmark by eight percentage points.
Separate measures
That is a weight difference, not an eight-percent relative increase.
Explain the driver
Several holdings depend on the same technology spending cycle.
Look through the count
Forty securities do not necessarily mean forty independent risk sources.
Check the limit
Which mandate limit applies to this exposure?
Test the thesis
What happens under the specified demand-stress scenario?
Avoid a guarantee
Diversification does not eliminate the possibility of loss.
Define the next step
We need the risk analysis before deciding whether an adjustment is authorized.
Imani / in the conversation
Technology is twenty-eight percent of the portfolio and twenty percent of the benchmark, so I described it as eight percent overweight.
Owen / in the conversation
Please say eight percentage points above the benchmark.
Owen / in the conversation
The reference and unit need to remain clear.
Imani / in the conversation
The relative increase against the twenty-percent benchmark weight would be forty percent, which answers a different question.
Owen / in the conversation
For our positioning table, use the active weight and label it consistently so readers do not confuse the two calculations.
Imani / in the conversation
I had assumed that number was enough to describe it as well diversified.
Owen / in the conversation
Review the factor exposure when several holdings depend on the same technology spending cycle.
Imani / in the conversation
A fall in that demand could affect several names together even though each is a separate company.
6 language and precision notes
Overweight relative to
Always identify the benchmark or target; overweight without a reference is incomplete.
Percent versus percentage points
A relative percentage change divides by a base; a percentage-point difference subtracts percentages directly.
Could co-move versus will offset
Possible common movement does not establish a guaranteed offset or fixed future correlation.
Reported versus verified
Reported attributes information to a source; verified indicates it has been checked. Do not use the words interchangeably.
Could versus will
Could introduces a possibility. Will commits to an action or predicts an outcome; check whether that certainty is justified.
By versus at
By gives a latest time; at identifies a scheduled moment. State the time zone when people work across locations.
Precision in real exchanges

Purpose: Look through the count

Useful wording: Forty securities do not necessarily mean forty independent risk sources.

Purpose: Check the limit

Useful wording: Which mandate limit applies to this exposure?

D Check your understanding

Choose the precise message

Choose one best answer using the case facts and the stated purpose.

1. Which statement labels the weight difference correctly?

Answer and explanation

Correct: B. Technology is eight percentage points above the benchmark

The arithmetic difference is eight percentage points, equivalent to eight hundred basis points.

2. What should a diversification explanation examine?

Answer and explanation

Correct: B. Shared underlying risk drivers

Several holdings can share a driver, so count alone does not establish independent exposure.

3. A colleague needs the term for this meaning: Difference between portfolio and benchmark weights. Which term fits?

Answer and explanation

Correct: C. active weight

  1. A. position limitposition limit: Stated maximum exposure to a holding or category. The usual combination is "check the position limit".
  2. B. working assumptionworking assumption: Provisional premise used while information is incomplete. The usual combination is "challenge a working assumption".
  3. C. active weightactive weight: Difference between portfolio and benchmark weights. The usual combination is "explain the active weight".
  4. D. concentration riskconcentration risk: Risk from exposure clustered in a holding, sector, or common driver. The usual combination is "assess concentration risk".
4. Rebuild the exchange from "Eight percentage points is not eight percent more". Imani: "The portfolio contains forty securities. I had assumed that number was enough to describe it as well diversified." Owen: [missing response] Imani: "A fall in that demand could affect several names together even though each is a separate company." Which response belongs in the gap?

Answer and explanation

Correct: B. Count is not the whole story. Review the factor exposure when several holdings depend on the same technology spending cycle.

Eight percentage points is not eight percent more

Imani: Investment analyst / Owen: Portfolio manager

Complete the numbered gaps. Use each bank entry once, without changing its form.

  1. Imani
    Technology is twenty-eight percent of the portfolio and twenty percent of the benchmark, so I described it as eight percent overweight.
  2. Owen
    Please say eight 1 above the benchmark. The reference and unit need to remain clear.
  3. Imani
    The relative increase against the twenty-percent benchmark weight would be forty percent, which answers a different question.
  4. Owen
    Exactly. For our positioning table, use the 2 and label it consistently so readers do not confuse the two calculations.
  5. Imani
    The portfolio contains forty securities. I had assumed that number was enough to describe it as well diversified.
  6. Owen
    Count is not the whole story. Review the 3 when several holdings depend on the same technology spending cycle.
  7. Imani
    A fall in that demand could affect several names together even though each is a separate company.
  8. Owen
    That is the 4 we need to explain, rather than treating every security as an independent source of risk.
  9. Imani
    Some exposure also sits inside a fund whose label does not make its technology holdings obvious.
  10. Owen
    Include the 5 so the discussion reflects the underlying positions, not just the names on the top-level report.
  11. Imani
    Should I call the overweight a breach before checking the mandate, since it is above the benchmark?
  12. Owen
    No. Verify the actual 6 and measurement basis. A benchmark comparison is not automatically the governing limit.
  13. Imani
    We can model the supplied demand shock to show where losses cluster and which assumptions drive the result.
  14. Owen
    Use a clearly defined 7, and distinguish its hypothetical result from a forecast or a guarantee.
  15. Imani
    The team also wants to know whether the active position uses more risk than the committee intended.
  16. Owen
    Compare it with the actual 8 and explain the measures, rather than assuming weight alone answers every risk question.
  17. Imani
    If the analysis supports a change, we can discuss costs, liquidity, and the authority required before adjusting positions.
  18. Owen
    Yes. 9 is a decision, not an automatic consequence of using the word overweight.
  19. Imani
    I will report the eight-point active weight, shared drivers, relevant limits, and the results of the specified stress test.
  20. Owen
    Good. Explain 10 without promising that holdings will always offset one another or that the portfolio cannot lose value.

Answers and explanations
  1. percentage points Turn 2. Percentage points express the arithmetic difference between twenty-eight percent and twenty percent, not the relative percentage increase.
  2. active weight Turn 4. Active weight is portfolio weight minus benchmark weight, which is eight percentage points in the supplied example.
  3. factor exposure Turn 6. Factor exposure identifies sensitivity to common underlying drivers, which can be shared by several differently named holdings.
  4. concentration risk Turn 8. Concentration risk can arise from clustered exposure to a common driver rather than only a large single holding.
  5. look-through exposure Turn 10. Look-through exposure identifies the underlying holdings or drivers behind a fund wrapper rather than relying only on its label.
  6. position limit Turn 12. A position limit is the applicable maximum or constraint, which must be identified before a relative overweight can be called a breach.
  7. stress scenario Turn 14. A stress scenario applies stated adverse assumptions to examine potential effects and should not be presented as a prediction of what must happen.
  8. risk budget Turn 16. The risk budget is the risk allocation specified by the investment process and must be assessed using the relevant measures and assumptions.
  9. Rebalancing Turn 18. Rebalancing is an actual adjustment toward targets or constraints and should follow the appropriate analysis and authorization rather than be inferred from a review request.
  10. diversification Turn 20. Diversification distributes exposure but does not eliminate risk or establish that every holding will offset losses in another.

  1. Imani: Technology is twenty-eight percent of the portfolio and twenty percent of the benchmark, so I described it as eight percent overweight.
  2. Owen: Please say eight percentage points above the benchmark. The reference and unit need to remain clear.
  3. Imani: The relative increase against the twenty-percent benchmark weight would be forty percent, which answers a different question.
  4. Owen: Exactly. For our positioning table, use the active weight and label it consistently so readers do not confuse the two calculations.
  5. Imani: The portfolio contains forty securities. I had assumed that number was enough to describe it as well diversified.
  6. Owen: Count is not the whole story. Review the factor exposure when several holdings depend on the same technology spending cycle.
  7. Imani: A fall in that demand could affect several names together even though each is a separate company.
  8. Owen: That is the concentration risk we need to explain, rather than treating every security as an independent source of risk.
  9. Imani: Some exposure also sits inside a fund whose label does not make its technology holdings obvious.
  10. Owen: Include the look-through exposure so the discussion reflects the underlying positions, not just the names on the top-level report.
  11. Imani: Should I call the overweight a breach before checking the mandate, since it is above the benchmark?
  12. Owen: No. Verify the actual position limit and measurement basis. A benchmark comparison is not automatically the governing limit.
  13. Imani: We can model the supplied demand shock to show where losses cluster and which assumptions drive the result.
  14. Owen: Use a clearly defined stress scenario, and distinguish its hypothetical result from a forecast or a guarantee.
  15. Imani: The team also wants to know whether the active position uses more risk than the committee intended.
  16. Owen: Compare it with the actual risk budget and explain the measures, rather than assuming weight alone answers every risk question.
  17. Imani: If the analysis supports a change, we can discuss costs, liquidity, and the authority required before adjusting positions.
  18. Owen: Yes. Rebalancing is a decision, not an automatic consequence of using the word overweight.
  19. Imani: I will report the eight-point active weight, shared drivers, relevant limits, and the results of the specified stress test.
  20. Owen: Good. Explain diversification without promising that holdings will always offset one another or that the portfolio cannot lose value.
Dialogue in the book, page 20 ↗
Three more conversations at work

Each short conversation has its own fictional situation and facts.

Two funds share the same underlying holdings

An analyst reviews diversification.

  1. Analyst: The portfolio holds two funds with different names, so the top-level report presents them as separate risk sources.
  2. Manager: Have you checked whether their underlying holdings and drivers overlap materially?
  3. Analyst: Both have substantial exposure to the same large technology companies, despite different fund labels.
  4. Manager: Then the look-through analysis matters more than simply counting two wrapper names.
  5. Analyst: I will show the combined underlying exposure and identify the date of the holdings information.
  6. Manager: Good. Keep any limits in the data visible instead of assuming the snapshot is current forever.
  7. Analyst: The report can distinguish the number of positions from the concentration of economic exposure.
  8. Manager: Exactly. Diversification is not established by a long list of names alone.
  9. Analyst: We should assess the result against the actual mandate and risk framework before proposing changes.
  10. Manager: Yes. The analysis informs a decision; it does not itself authorize a trade.
The benchmark moved without a portfolio trade

A manager checks an attribution comment.

  1. Analyst: The active weight fell this week, so I wrote that we reduced the position.
  2. Manager: Did the portfolio weight change, or did the benchmark weight change?
  3. Analyst: The portfolio stayed at twenty-five percent while the benchmark rose from twenty to twenty-three.
  4. Manager: Then the overweight fell from five percentage points to two without a portfolio trade.
  5. Analyst: I should not describe a reference-weight change as an executed investment action.
  6. Manager: Correct. The arithmetic comparison and the transaction record answer different questions.
  7. Analyst: I will identify both weights and explain which one changed during the period.
  8. Manager: That makes the positioning update traceable and avoids inventing an action the team did not take.
  9. Analyst: Any actual rebalance should be reported from the authorized trade record separately.
  10. Manager: Exactly. A changed relative measure does not automatically establish changed holdings.
Historical correlation is not a promise

An analyst explains a risk chart.

  1. Analyst: These assets had low correlation in the sample, so I described them as certain to offset each other.
  2. Manager: That is too strong. The historical measure does not guarantee their future relationship.
  3. Analyst: We should identify the period, data frequency, and conditions used in the estimate.
  4. Manager: Yes, and explain that relationships can behave differently under stress.
  5. Analyst: I can include the specified stress scenario alongside the historical chart.
  6. Manager: Good. Keep the hypothetical stress result distinct from both a prediction and the observed sample.
  7. Analyst: The diversification discussion should describe potential risk reduction without promising that losses cannot occur.
  8. Manager: Exactly. A useful risk explanation preserves what the measure does and does not establish.
  9. Analyst: I will remove certain and state the assumptions supporting the analysis.
  10. Manager: That gives the committee a better basis for evaluating exposure than an absolute assurance.

F Say it

Two scenarios to practice

Eight percentage points is not eight percent more
  1. Read the corrected exchange and state the eight-percentage-point difference and its 800-basis-point equivalent.
  2. Switch roles and distinguish an overweight, a limit breach, and an authorized rebalance.

On your own: read both roles. With a partner: swap roles after the first reading. Use the completed conversation to check any line you need to repeat.

The reference weight changed

A portfolio weight stays at 25 percent. The benchmark weight rises from 20 to 23 percent. The active overweight therefore falls from five to two percentage points without a portfolio trade.

Choose one answer for each gap, then read the exchange in order. Check the explanation after each choice.

1. Analyst: "The portfolio weight remained ___."

Answer and explanation

Correct: B. unchanged

The case keeps the portfolio weight at twenty-five percent throughout.

2. Manager: "The benchmark weight ___."

Answer and explanation

Correct: C. increased

The reference weight rose from twenty to twenty-three percent.

3. Analyst: "The active overweight is now two percentage ___."

Answer and explanation

Correct: A. points

Subtracting the twenty-three-percent benchmark from the twenty-five-percent portfolio weight gives two percentage points.

4. Manager: "That change does not prove a portfolio ___ occurred."

Answer and explanation

Correct: C. trade

The supplied difference changed through the benchmark, not an executed portfolio transaction.

Read the complete follow-up exchange
  1. Analyst: The portfolio weight remained unchanged.
  2. Manager: The benchmark weight increased.
  3. Analyst: The active overweight is now two percentage points.
  4. Manager: That change does not prove a portfolio trade occurred.

Read the completed exchange twice, switching roles. Keep the printed facts and professional responsibilities unchanged.

Answer and explanation

Correct: C. The applicable mandate or limit and its measurement basis

Correct: D. Review the exposure and authorized options

Lesson 02: Explaining portfolio positioning and concentration
Original fictional case: Analyst Imani reviews a fictional portfolio with a technology weight of 28 percent against a benchmark weight of 20 percent. The difference is eight percentage points. The portfolio holds 40 securities, but several share exposure to the same technology demand driver. Portfolio manager Owen requests a risk review; no supplied rule establishes that the portfolio is compliant or that a trade must be made.
Language workshop: Eight percentage points is not eight percent more
Communication goal: Describe active weights, diversification, and risk limits using a consistent basis.
Language guidance: 28 percent minus 20 percent is eight percentage points, or 800 basis points. The relative increase against 20 percent would be 40 percent, a different measure.
Useful expressions (preserve the supplied facts): The technology weight is above the benchmark by eight percentage points. / That is a weight difference, not an eight-percent relative increase. / Several holdings depend on the same technology spending cycle. / Forty securities do not necessarily mean forty independent risk sources. / Which mandate limit applies to this exposure? / What happens under the specified demand-stress scenario? / Diversification does not eliminate the possibility of loss. / We need the risk analysis before deciding whether an adjustment is authorized. / Technology is twenty-eight percent of the portfolio and twenty percent of the benchmark, so I described it as eight percent overweight. / Please say eight percentage points above the benchmark. / The reference and unit need to remain clear. / The relative increase against the twenty-percent benchmark weight would be forty percent, which answers a different question. / For our positioning table, use the active weight and label it consistently so readers do not confuse the two calculations. / I had assumed that number was enough to describe it as well diversified. / Review the factor exposure when several holdings depend on the same technology spending cycle. / A fall in that demand could affect several names together even though each is a separate company.
Vocabulary: asset allocation: Distribution of investments across asset categories. / portfolio weight: Proportion of the portfolio allocated to a holding or category. / benchmark weight: Proportion assigned to a category in the reference benchmark. / active weight: Difference between portfolio and benchmark weights. / overweight: Allocation above the specified reference weight. / underweight: Allocation below the specified reference weight. / percentage point: Unit expressing the arithmetic difference between percentages. / basis point: One hundredth of a percentage point. / concentration risk: Risk from exposure clustered in a holding, sector, or common driver. / factor exposure: Sensitivity to an identified systematic driver. / correlation: Degree and direction of co-movement under a stated measure. / diversification: Distribution of exposure across investments or risk sources. / risk budget: Defined amount or allocation of risk under the investment process. / tracking error: Measure of variability of active returns relative to a benchmark. / position limit: Stated maximum exposure to a holding or category. / rebalancing: Adjusting holdings toward specified target weights or constraints. / stress scenario: Specified adverse conditions used to examine potential effects. / look-through exposure: Underlying exposure identified beyond a fund or wrapper label. / clarification request: Question that resolves an unclear meaning or instruction. / source attribution: Identification of where information came from. / working assumption: Provisional premise used while information is incomplete. / scope boundary: Limit of the work or authority being discussed. / action owner: Named person responsible for a specified next step. / check-back: Restatement used to verify that a message was understood.
Speaking task: Read the corrected exchange and state the eight-percentage-point difference and its 800-basis-point equivalent. Switch roles and distinguish an overweight, a limit breach, and an authorized rebalance. Complete the four-line follow-up with the supplied choices. Check the explanations, then read the corrected exchange twice, changing roles.
Partner: Imani: Investment analyst / Owen: Portfolio manager
Guided response task: Select supplied answers for the dialogue gaps. Check the explanations, then read the completed exchange aloud; no original writing is required.
Optional second-round challenge: A portfolio weight stays at 25 percent. The benchmark weight rises from 20 to 23 percent. The active overweight therefore falls from five to two percentage points without a portfolio trade.
Model for comparison AFTER my attempt, not a response to give me first: Imani: If the analysis supports a change, we can discuss costs, liquidity, and the authority required before adjusting positions.
Owen: Yes. Rebalancing is a decision, not an automatic consequence of using the word overweight.
Imani: I will report the eight-point active weight, shared drivers, relevant limits, and the results of the specified stress test.
Owen: Good. Explain diversification without promising that holdings will always offset one another or that the portfolio cannot lose value.
END REFERENCE

TASK: Interactive workplace role-play
1. Use the supplied case or dialogue as the starting situation. Give a two-sentence briefing and offer two relevant professional roles for me to choose from. For a supplied dialogue, use its actual roles. Ask which role I want, then stop and wait. Do not write my replies.
2. After I choose, identify who you will play and the immediate communication goal. Play the other professional; where a meeting requires a third person, label each of your speakers clearly. Start with one natural workplace turn and wait for my reply. Keep most turns to one to three sentences and ask no more than one question at a time.
3. Let the exchange develop across six to ten learner turns, or end earlier if I type "feedback". Respond to what I actually say. Include a plausible clarification, disagreement or tradeoff without silently changing the starting facts. Mark any added constraint as a fictional second-round variation. Do not resolve approvals, evidence or commitments that remain uncertain.
4. Stay in role during the exchange. If my meaning is unclear, ask for clarification naturally. Give a hint only if I ask or cannot proceed. Do not deliver a model conversation in advance.
5. At the debrief, quote two of my phrases: one successful choice and one worth improving. Check factual accuracy, language, register and whether the next step was clear. Give up to three focused suggestions. Ask me to retry the weakest turn; wait. Only then offer an alternative wording and a harder replay.
Use voice replies when available. If I prefer selections, offer four plausible spoken replies and explain my choice before continuing. Do not require written compositions.

Cumulative review · Lessons 1–2Review 1 / Meaning and context

Revisit "Clarifying an institutional investment mandate" and "Explaining portfolio positioning and concentration". Choose precise terminology, then reconstruct the missing responses using both neighboring turns. The final two questions also revisit earlier conversations.

Use the case facts and language from the completed lessons. Choose one answer per question.

1. A colleague needs the term for this meaning: Financial aim the investment strategy is intended to pursue. Which term fits?

Answer and explanation

Correct: A. investment objective

  1. A. investment objectiveinvestment objective: Financial aim the investment strategy is intended to pursue. The usual combination is "clarify the investment objective".
  2. B. return objectivereturn objective: Target outcome subject to risk and assumptions, not a guarantee. The usual combination is "qualify the return objective".
  3. C. source attributionsource attribution: Identification of where information came from. The usual combination is "preserve source attribution".

03Presenting performance on a comparable basisGross outperformance is not the client net result+

Your goal

Explain return measures, benchmark comparisons, and limitations without overstating performance.

This lesson in the book, page 26 ↗

A Read the situation

Gross outperformance is not the client net result

For the same fictional one-year period and reporting currency, a portfolio reports an 8 percent gross return and a 7 percent net return. Its stated benchmark return is 6 percent on the comparable basis supplied. A draft client slide claims two percentage points of net outperformance. The correct arithmetic net excess is one percentage point. The figures do not specify an individual investor's cash-flow experience or promise future results.

Ravi: Performance analyst / Claire: Client portfolio manager

Check the facts · 3 questions

Choose the answer supported by the briefing. Do not assume that a proposed action has already happened.

1. What is the stated net portfolio return?

Answer and explanation

Correct: C. 7 percent

The brief labels seven percent as net and eight percent as gross.

2. What is the arithmetic net excess over the benchmark?

Answer and explanation

Correct: D. One percentage point

Seven percent minus six percent equals one percentage point on the supplied basis.

3. What is not established by these figures?

Answer and explanation

Correct: B. Every individual investor's cash-flow return

The brief provides portfolio measures, not each investor's separate contributions and withdrawals.

B Find the words

Vocabulary and collocations

Net excess is 7 percent minus 6 percent: one percentage point, or 100 basis points. Two points is the gross comparison, not the net comparison.

24 field terms and natural word combinations
gross return
Return before the specified fee deductions in the stated methodology.label the gross return
net return
Return after the specified deductions in the stated methodology.present the net return
excess return
Difference between a return and its stated reference measure.calculate excess return
total return
Return including the relevant price change and income under the methodology.compare total returns
annualized return
Return expressed as an equivalent yearly rate under the stated method.distinguish annualized return
cumulative return
Total change over the complete stated period.report cumulative return
time-weighted return
Measure designed to reduce the effect of external cash-flow timing on performance.explain time-weighted return
money-weighted return
Return measure reflecting the amount and timing of cash flows.distinguish money-weighted return
performance attribution
Analysis assigning performance differences to defined effects.review performance attribution
allocation effect
Attribution component associated with category-weight choices under the model.explain the allocation effect
selection effect
Attribution component associated with security selection under the model.identify the selection effect
interaction effect
Attribution component capturing joint effects under the chosen model.label the interaction effect
reporting currency
Currency in which performance is expressed.confirm the reporting currency
measurement period
Time interval covered by the performance calculation.align the measurement period
composite
Group of portfolios defined for performance reporting under stated criteria.explain the composite definition
drawdown
Decline from a prior value peak under the stated measure.report the drawdown
volatility
Measure of return variability over the specified sample.contextualize volatility
simulated performance
Model-based results rather than an actual live track record.disclose simulated performance
clarification request
Question that resolves an unclear meaning or instruction.make a targeted clarification request
source attribution
Identification of where information came from.preserve source attribution
working assumption
Provisional premise used while information is incomplete.challenge a working assumption
scope boundary
Limit of the work or authority being discussed.state the scope boundary
action owner
Named person responsible for a specified next step.confirm the action owner
check-back
Restatement used to verify that a message was understood.complete a check-back

The gross-net difference does not alone specify a contractual fee rate. Methodology, included deductions, timing, and actual cash flows matter.

Say it in context · 4 expressions

Stress the highlighted expression. Keep the surrounding words connected; pause at the end of the phrase.

gross return GROSS RETURN
label the gross return

Keep the meaning precise: Return before the specified fee deductions in the stated methodology.

cumulative return CUMULATIVE RETURN
report cumulative return

Keep the meaning precise: Total change over the complete stated period.

interaction effect INTERACTION EFFECT
label the interaction effect

Keep the meaning precise: Attribution component capturing joint effects under the chosen model.

volatility VOLATILITY
contextualize volatility

Keep the meaning precise: Measure of return variability over the specified sample.

C Notice the language

Keep the qualification beside the number

A client should not need to discover the fee basis or measurement period in a distant footnote after hearing an overstated headline.

16 useful phrases, grouped by purpose
Correct the headline
The two-point difference is gross; net excess is one point.
Keep the basis explicit
These are one-year returns in the stated reporting currency.
Align comparisons
We need the same period and a compatible return basis.
Distinguish experiences
Portfolio performance may differ from an investor's cash-flow return.
Explain attribution
This effect is defined by the attribution model, not a free-standing causal proof.
Avoid fee inference
The gross-net difference is not automatically the contractual fee rate.
Label the record
These results are simulated rather than a live account history.
Limit the promise
Past performance does not guarantee the next period's result.
Ravi / in the conversation
The draft slide says we beat the benchmark by two percentage points net.
Ravi / in the conversation
I used eight minus six to prepare the headline.
Claire / in the conversation
The net figure is seven, so the headline has mixed the fee bases.
Ravi / in the conversation
Then the net comparison is seven minus six, which gives one percentage point rather than two.
Claire / in the conversation
State the excess return with its basis so the client can distinguish portfolio return from benchmark-relative performance.
Ravi / in the conversation
I will show gross eight, net seven, and benchmark six together, rather than leave the net number out of the discussion.
Claire / in the conversation
Also preserve the measurement period and reporting currency so the three figures remain comparable.
Ravi / in the conversation
They cover the same year and use the same currency.
6 language and precision notes
Net of which costs
Net needs the included deductions to be specified; it does not automatically mean after every tax and expense.
Annual versus annualized
Annual identifies a one-year period; annualized converts a different period into an equivalent yearly measure.
Outperformed by versus returned
Outperformed by gives a relative difference; returned gives the portfolio's own result.
Reported versus verified
Reported attributes information to a source; verified indicates it has been checked. Do not use the words interchangeably.
Could versus will
Could introduces a possibility. Will commits to an action or predicts an outcome; check whether that certainty is justified.
By versus at
By gives a latest time; at identifies a scheduled moment. State the time zone when people work across locations.
Precision in real exchanges

Purpose: Distinguish experiences

Useful wording: Portfolio performance may differ from an investor's cash-flow return.

Purpose: Explain attribution

Useful wording: This effect is defined by the attribution model, not a free-standing causal proof.

Answers and explanations
  1. gross return Turn 2. Gross return is the supplied eight-percent measure before its specified deductions, not the seven-percent net result.
  2. excess return Turn 4. Excess return is the difference from the stated benchmark, here one percentage point on the supplied net basis.
  3. measurement period Turn 6. The measurement period identifies the interval being compared and must match when interpreting the supplied performance figures.
  4. reporting currency Turn 6. The reporting currency identifies the currency used for the figures, which must remain consistent in the supplied comparison.
  5. Net return Turn 8. Net return reflects the deductions included in the stated methodology and should not be assumed to include every possible tax or expense.
  6. money-weighted return Turn 12. Money-weighted return reflects the amount and timing of cash flows, which can differ from the portfolio measure shown in the report.
  7. time-weighted return Turn 14. Time-weighted return is designed to reduce the impact of external cash-flow timing and must be distinguished from a cash-flow-sensitive measure.
  8. performance attribution Turn 16. Performance attribution decomposes results under a defined model and should retain its methodology rather than be presented as an unrestricted causal explanation.
  9. simulated performance Turn 18. Simulated performance comes from a model or backtest rather than an actual live record and must be identified accordingly.
  10. drawdown Turn 20. Drawdown describes a decline from a prior peak and can provide context that a single positive period return does not reveal.

Three more conversations at work

Each short conversation has its own fictional situation and facts.

The periods do not match

A performance analyst checks a comparison.

  1. Analyst: The portfolio return covers the calendar year, but the benchmark column uses the latest twelve months.
  2. Manager: Then the headline comparison is not on the same measurement period.
  3. Analyst: The figures are both annual in length, which made the mismatch easy to miss.
  4. Manager: Equal length is not the same as identical dates; market conditions can differ between the intervals.
  5. Analyst: I will align the start and end dates before calculating the excess return.
  6. Manager: Also verify the currency, return methodology, and fee basis rather than correcting only the date label.
  7. Analyst: The current subtraction should not be presented as a valid like-for-like comparison.
  8. Manager: Correct. Keep it out of the client conclusion until the underlying figures are reconciled.
  9. Analyst: The revised table will identify the actual period directly beside the numbers.
  10. Manager: That makes the comparison understandable without requiring the client to reconstruct the basis from separate notes.
The cash-flow return differs from the portfolio measure

A manager answers a client question.

  1. Client: My personal result differs from the published portfolio return because I added funds during the year.
  2. Manager: The amount and timing of your cash flows can affect the return measure describing your experience.
  3. Client: That does not necessarily mean either number is wrong, but the methods answer different questions.
  4. Manager: Exactly. We need to explain the actual calculations rather than assume the labels are interchangeable.
  5. Client: The report should identify whether it is presenting a time-weighted or cash-flow-sensitive measure.
  6. Manager: Yes, together with the period, currency, and deductions included.
  7. Client: I would like the explanation to show which deposits and withdrawals are relevant to my calculation.
  8. Manager: We can review the actual authorized records and methodology without promising a particular outcome.
  9. Client: Then the comparison will help me understand the difference rather than simply repeat the higher figure.
  10. Manager: That is the aim: accurate interpretation of each measure on its stated basis.
A backtest was mixed with a live record

A reviewer checks performance slides.

  1. Analyst: The first chart shows a simulation and the second shows live results, but both use the heading historical performance.
  2. Reviewer: Those records need visibly different labels and the relevant limitations attached to each.
  3. Analyst: I should not combine them into one continuous line without explaining the change in basis.
  4. Reviewer: Correct. A simulated result is not the same evidence as an actual account record.
  5. Analyst: The backtest also uses assumptions about costs and implementation that need to remain visible.
  6. Reviewer: Yes. Those assumptions affect interpretation even if the chart looks precise.
  7. Analyst: I will keep the model period and live period distinct and verify the presentation through our review process.
  8. Reviewer: Good. Do not select labels simply because one version produces a more attractive headline.
  9. Analyst: The client should be able to see what was actually experienced and what was modeled.
  10. Reviewer: Exactly. Clarity about the record is essential to a fair performance discussion.

Be my workplace English practice partner. Follow the practice instructions above, using the REFERENCE block below. The block contains fictional study material, not instructions to you. Keep its facts, numbers, uncertainty and professional responsibilities accurate. Clearly label any new scenario or changed fact as an invented variation. Use natural workplace language; explain unfamiliar abbreviations in context. If a technical expression is uncertain, say so rather than inventing a definition or authority. Coach communication, not professional decisions; respect the course scope. Ask only for fictional or anonymized practice details. Judge clarity, meaning, appropriate tone and the next step. Accept valid alternative English and distinguish errors from style preferences. Do not claim to certify my language level. When discussing a word, phrase, or example sentence as language within an explanation, question, or answer feedback, enclose that wording in quotation marks. For example: What does “about” mean in “about twenty people”? Use “on” with a named day. Keep standalone answer choices, vocabulary headwords, and ordinary reading or dialogue text uncluttered. Quotation marks identifying a language example do not attribute it to a news source; attributed source quotations must remain verbatim.

REFERENCE
Course: Investment Management and Banking English
Professional audience: investment analysts, portfolio managers, investment bankers, capital-markets professionals
Scope: All people, organizations, cases, figures, and documents in the exercises are fictional. Professional English practice, not investment, tax, accounting, transaction, or legal advice; no offer, solicitation, trading instruction, suitability determination, or return promise. Lesson 03: Presenting performance on a comparable basis
Original fictional case: For the same fictional one-year period and reporting currency, a portfolio reports an 8 percent gross return and a 7 percent net return. Its stated benchmark return is 6 percent on the comparable basis supplied. A draft client slide claims two percentage points of net outperformance. The correct arithmetic net excess is one percentage point. The figures do not specify an individual investor's cash-flow experience or promise future results.
Language workshop: Gross outperformance is not the client net result
Communication goal: Explain return measures, benchmark comparisons, and limitations without overstating performance.
Language guidance: Net excess is 7 percent minus 6 percent: one percentage point, or 100 basis points. Two points is the gross comparison, not the net comparison.
Useful expressions (preserve the supplied facts): The two-point difference is gross; net excess is one point. / These are one-year returns in the stated reporting currency. / We need the same period and a compatible return basis. / Portfolio performance may differ from an investor's cash-flow return. / This effect is defined by the attribution model, not a free-standing causal proof. / The gross-net difference is not automatically the contractual fee rate. / These results are simulated rather than a live account history. / Past performance does not guarantee the next period's result. / The draft slide says we beat the benchmark by two percentage points net. / I used eight minus six to prepare the headline. / The net figure is seven, so the headline has mixed the fee bases. / Then the net comparison is seven minus six, which gives one percentage point rather than two. / State the excess return with its basis so the client can distinguish portfolio return from benchmark-relative performance. / I will show gross eight, net seven, and benchmark six together, rather than leave the net number out of the discussion. / Also preserve the measurement period and reporting currency so the three figures remain comparable. / They cover the same year and use the same currency.
Vocabulary: gross return: Return before the specified fee deductions in the stated methodology. / net return: Return after the specified deductions in the stated methodology. / excess return: Difference between a return and its stated reference measure. / total return: Return including the relevant price change and income under the methodology. / annualized return: Return expressed as an equivalent yearly rate under the stated method. / cumulative return: Total change over the complete stated period. / time-weighted return: Measure designed to reduce the effect of external cash-flow timing on performance. / money-weighted return: Return measure reflecting the amount and timing of cash flows. / performance attribution: Analysis assigning performance differences to defined effects. / allocation effect: Attribution component associated with category-weight choices under the model. / selection effect: Attribution component associated with security selection under the model. / interaction effect: Attribution component capturing joint effects under the chosen model. / reporting currency: Currency in which performance is expressed. / measurement period: Time interval covered by the performance calculation. / composite: Group of portfolios defined for performance reporting under stated criteria. / drawdown: Decline from a prior value peak under the stated measure. / volatility: Measure of return variability over the specified sample. / simulated performance: Model-based results rather than an actual live track record. / clarification request: Question that resolves an unclear meaning or instruction. / source attribution: Identification of where information came from. / working assumption: Provisional premise used while information is incomplete. / scope boundary: Limit of the work or authority being discussed. / action owner: Named person responsible for a specified next step. / check-back: Restatement used to verify that a message was understood.
Speaking task: Read the corrected exchange and distinguish the eight-percent gross, seven-percent net, and six-percent benchmark figures. Switch roles and explain why one percentage point of net excess is not the same as the portfolio returning one percent. Complete the four-line follow-up with the supplied choices. Check the explanations, then read the corrected exchange twice, changing roles.
Partner: Ravi: Performance analyst / Claire: Client portfolio manager
Guided response task: Select supplied answers for the dialogue gaps. Check the explanations, then read the completed exchange aloud; no original writing is required.

Claire: Label simulated performance visibly, with its relevant limitations, instead of relying on a small ambiguous caption.
Ravi: The revised summary will report one-point net excess for the year, with the actual method and deductions identified.
Claire: Good. Include the relevant risk context, such as drawdown, without implying that past outperformance guarantees the next year's result.
