Dialogue 05: The headline value is not the seller proceeds
Original fictional setting: Investment banker Eva explains an illustrative valuation to corporate client Theo. The model uses normalized EBITDA of USD 15 million at an 8-times multiple, implying enterprise value of USD 120 million. It then subtracts debt of USD 30 million and adds eligible cash of USD 10 million, giving equity value of USD 100 million. No other adjustments are included in this simplified bridge. The EBITDA normalization is still under diligence, and seller taxes, fees, and actual proceeds are not calculated.
Professional roles: Theo / Eva
Published dialogue (reference script, not my own performance):
Theo: The presentation says one hundred twenty million dollars. Is that what the shareholders will receive when the transaction closes?
Eva: That headline is enterprise value in our illustration. We need to walk from that measure to equity value and then distinguish actual proceeds.
Theo: You arrived at the headline by multiplying fifteen million of normalized EBITDA by eight, correct?
Eva: Yes. Eight is the valuation multiple applied to the stated metric, with both the metric and the comparison basis requiring clear definitions.
Theo: The fifteen-million figure includes adjustments management proposed. I do not want the model to imply they have all been verified.
Eva: It should not. Normalized EBITDA remains subject to diligence, and it is not the same thing as cash available to shareholders.
Theo: For the bridge, the example includes thirty million of debt and ten million of cash that is eligible under the stated definition.
Eva: Correct. The equity bridge subtracts thirty from one hundred twenty and adds ten, giving one hundred million.
Theo: We could also describe the adjustment as subtracting twenty million of net debt, provided we use the same definition.
Eva: Exactly. Net debt is twenty in this simplified case. Do not then subtract the thirty again, because that would double count.
Theo: What makes the cash eligible? I know some transaction definitions distinguish accessible cash from restricted balances.
Eva: The actual terms determine eligible cash. Here we explicitly supply ten for the exercise, but a real bridge needs the relevant definitions and verification.
Theo: The illustration says no other adjustments. Does that mean real transactions never have additional claims or price mechanisms?
Eva: No. A debt-like item or other adjustment can matter in the actual terms. The illustration excludes them; it does not declare them irrelevant everywhere.
Theo: Then the one-hundred-million result is equity value under these supplied assumptions, not a complete closing statement.
Eva: Yes. Seller proceeds can differ because of costs, taxes, and other actual transaction effects not calculated here.
Theo: I also want the comparison slide to show whether the other deals use the same earnings definition and time period.
Eva: That is essential when using precedent transactions. A similar headline multiple can conceal different metrics, periods, or deal circumstances.
Theo: I will summarize the model as illustrative enterprise value of one hundred twenty and equity value of one hundred, with normalization still under review.
Eva: Good. Keep equity value, the unresolved inputs, and the uncalculated proceeds separate, so the board understands exactly what the numbers do and do not represent.
Vocabulary in this exchange: enterprise value: Value measure for the operating business under the stated definition. / equity value: Value attributable to equity after the relevant bridge adjustments. / EBITDA: Earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization under the stated calculation. / normalized EBITDA: EBITDA adjusted for specified items under a stated normalization approach. / valuation multiple: Ratio applied to a specified financial metric. / net debt: Defined debt less eligible cash under the stated calculation.
END REFERENCE

Dialogue 06: Repeat purchases are not necessarily contracted recurring revenue
Original fictional setting: In a fictional sell-side transaction, management reports USD 100 million of last-twelve-month revenue, including USD 30 million from one customer. A slide calls that customer revenue contracted recurring revenue. The data room contains past invoices but no reviewed renewal contract for the next period. Banker Lena and finance lead Omar must describe the gap without concluding that no contract exists or that all revenue will disappear.
Professional roles: Omar / Lena
Published dialogue (reference script, not my own performance):
Omar: The customer has bought from us repeatedly, so the slide describes its thirty million dollars as contracted recurring revenue.
Lena: What supports that contracted recurring revenue label? We have reviewed invoices, but not a renewal agreement for the next period.
Omar: The invoices support the historical revenue. I agree they do not by themselves show the terms of a future commitment.
Lena: Exactly. A repeat purchase and a contractual renewal are different pieces of evidence.
Omar: Our total revenue for the trailing period is one hundred million, with thirty million from this customer.
Lena: That creates material customer concentration to discuss: thirty percent of the supplied revenue comes from this relationship.
Omar: We should identify the period carefully, because the same slide also includes a current-year management forecast.
Lena: Keep last-twelve-month revenue separate from the forecast so the audience does not mistake projected sales for recognized historical revenue.
Omar: The commercial team may have the agreement in another approved location. Its absence from this folder does not prove it does not exist.
Lena: Correct. Update the diligence request list with the precise document and terms needed for review.
Omar: I will ask for the agreement, any amendments, the relevant term, and the conditions governing renewal or termination.
Lena: Route them through the controlled data room and appropriate legal and commercial review, rather than emailing confidential material indiscriminately.
Omar: Another sheet uses bookings to support the same revenue number. We should not treat those figures as identical without checking.
Lena: Yes. Bookings, backlog, and recognized revenue need their own definitions and reconciliation.
Omar: We also show a retention percentage, but I need to confirm whether it includes expansion from existing customers.
Lena: That matters for net revenue retention. Keep the cohort, period, and treatment of expansion clear before comparing it with another metric.
Omar: I can attribute the current contract description to management while making the evidence gap visible in the diligence update.
Lena: Good. A management representation should not become an independently verified fact merely because we repeat it in the transaction materials.
Omar: The revised note will quantify the concentration, distinguish history from forecast, and mark contract support as outstanding.
Lena: That is an appropriate diligence red flag to investigate, without asserting that no agreement exists or predicting that every dollar of future revenue will disappear.
Vocabulary in this exchange: data room: Controlled repository of transaction information. / diligence request list: Record of information requested for the review. / last-twelve-month revenue: Revenue for the specified trailing twelve-month period. / customer concentration: Dependence on revenue or business from a limited customer group. / contracted recurring revenue: Revenue described as recurring under actual contractual terms and definitions. / repeat purchase: Another purchase that does not alone establish a future contractual commitment.
END REFERENCE

Dialogue 07: A one-and-a-half-times book is not cash received
Original fictional setting: In a fictional offering illustration, the target gross deal size is USD 80 million: USD 60 million of new shares and USD 20 million sold by existing shareholders. Nonbinding indications of interest total USD 120 million on the same provisional pricing basis. No final allocation, pricing, or settlement has occurred. Fees and expenses are excluded from the figures.
Professional roles: Mina / James
Published dialogue (reference script, not my own performance):
Mina: We have one hundred twenty million dollars of interest for an eighty-million-dollar offering. Can we announce that the funding is secured?
James: Not from these indications of interest. The demand is nonbinding and uses the current provisional pricing basis.
Mina: We can still describe the indicated book as one and a half times the target, provided those qualifications stay attached.
James: Yes. The order book is a useful demand signal, not a record of cash already received.
Mina: The target consists of sixty million of new shares and twenty million sold by existing shareholders.
James: Then the primary shares generate the issuer component, while the existing-holder sale is separate.
Mina: Some colleagues have described the full eighty million as money available for the company's expansion plan.
James: That ignores the secondary shares. The twenty-million component goes to the selling shareholders before the relevant costs.
Mina: We also have not deducted fees or expenses, so even the sixty-million issuer figure is gross.
James: Correct. Issuer proceeds need both distinctions: who receives the money and which deductions the figure includes.
Mina: Investors may change their demand when they see the final price or terms, even if the initial conversations were encouraging.
James: Exactly. The final offering price and terms are not established merely by the current demand total.
Mina: The team should also avoid telling an interested investor that a specific amount is reserved before the allocation process is complete.
James: Yes. Allocation is a separate stage, and any statement must reflect the actual authority and status.
Mina: Does the bank's involvement mean it is automatically obligated to purchase any securities investors do not take?
James: We need the underwriting agreement. The role and commitment depend on its terms, not on a general label.
Mina: We will use the reviewed offering materials rather than improvise claims about guaranteed demand or future trading performance.
James: Good. The prospectus and other authorized communications need to be consistent with the actual facts and applicable rules.
Mina: My update will say indicated demand is 1.5 times the target, with pricing, allocation, and settlement still outstanding.
James: That accurately describes bookbuilding progress while preserving execution uncertainty and the difference between the total deal and the issuer's gross primary proceeds.
Vocabulary in this exchange: issuer: Entity offering the relevant securities. / bookbuilding: Gathering investor demand information for an offering. / order book: Compilation of demand information under the offering process. / allocation: Assignment of offered securities under the actual process. / primary shares: Newly issued shares sold by the company in the offering. / secondary shares: Existing shares sold by current holders in the offering.
END REFERENCE

Dialogue 07: A one-and-a-half-times book is not cash received
Original fictional setting: In a fictional offering illustration, the target gross deal size is USD 80 million: USD 60 million of new shares and USD 20 million sold by existing shareholders. Nonbinding indications of interest total USD 120 million on the same provisional pricing basis. No final allocation, pricing, or settlement has occurred. Fees and expenses are excluded from the figures.
Professional roles: Mina / James
Published dialogue (reference script, not my own performance):
Mina: We have one hundred twenty million dollars of interest for an eighty-million-dollar offering. Can we announce that the funding is secured?
James: Not from these indications of interest. The demand is nonbinding and uses the current provisional pricing basis.
Mina: We can still describe the indicated book as one and a half times the target, provided those qualifications stay attached.
James: Yes. The order book is a useful demand signal, not a record of cash already received.
Mina: The target consists of sixty million of new shares and twenty million sold by existing shareholders.
James: Then the primary shares generate the issuer component, while the existing-holder sale is separate.
Mina: Some colleagues have described the full eighty million as money available for the company's expansion plan.
James: That ignores the secondary shares. The twenty-million component goes to the selling shareholders before the relevant costs.
Mina: We also have not deducted fees or expenses, so even the sixty-million issuer figure is gross.
James: Correct. Issuer proceeds need both distinctions: who receives the money and which deductions the figure includes.
Mina: Investors may change their demand when they see the final price or terms, even if the initial conversations were encouraging.
James: Exactly. The final offering price and terms are not established merely by the current demand total.
Mina: The team should also avoid telling an interested investor that a specific amount is reserved before the allocation process is complete.
James: Yes. Allocation is a separate stage, and any statement must reflect the actual authority and status.
Mina: Does the bank's involvement mean it is automatically obligated to purchase any securities investors do not take?
James: We need the underwriting agreement. The role and commitment depend on its terms, not on a general label.
Mina: We will use the reviewed offering materials rather than improvise claims about guaranteed demand or future trading performance.
James: Good. The prospectus and other authorized communications need to be consistent with the actual facts and applicable rules.
Mina: My update will say indicated demand is 1.5 times the target, with pricing, allocation, and settlement still outstanding.
James: That accurately describes bookbuilding progress while preserving execution uncertainty and the difference between the total deal and the issuer's gross primary proceeds.
Vocabulary in this exchange: issuer: Entity offering the relevant securities. / bookbuilding: Gathering investor demand information for an offering. / order book: Compilation of demand information under the offering process. / allocation: Assignment of offered securities under the actual process. / primary shares: Newly issued shares sold by the company in the offering. / secondary shares: Existing shares sold by current holders in the offering.
END REFERENCE

Dialogue 08: A public rumor does not release a private fact
Original fictional setting: Banking analyst Dev works on confidential transaction material. A colleague in an investment team asks whether a public acquisition rumor is true, hoping to inform a portfolio decision. Dev has not been authorized to share the material or confirm the transaction. Compliance officer Rosa explains the need to preserve information barriers and use the actual escalation process. The case supplies no legal determination that information is public or permission to trade.
Professional roles: Dev / Rosa
Published dialogue (reference script, not my own performance):
Dev: A colleague on the investment team asked whether an acquisition rumor is true. They know I work on confidential transaction material.
Rosa: Do not confirm or hint at the answer. Your client confidentiality obligations remain relevant even when the question starts with public speculation.
Dev: I was going to say I could not send the documents but could give a quick verbal sense of whether the story was accurate.
Rosa: That could still cross the information barrier. Protecting the attachment while revealing its substance does not preserve the boundary.
Dev: The colleague argues that we work for the same organization and that the information could improve a portfolio decision.
Rosa: Shared employment does not establish need-to-know access for that activity. Banking access and portfolio-research access serve different authorized purposes.
Dev: I should decline without saying anything that confirms whether the rumored transaction is one of our confidential matters.
Rosa: Exactly. Use compliance escalation for the request rather than decide on your own that an informal answer is harmless.
Dev: Does a newspaper rumor mean the information is now public enough for the team to use without further checking?
Rosa: A rumor is not proof of public dissemination of the verified facts. The actual information and legal or policy position need review.
Dev: We should treat the material as potentially sensitive rather than make our own quick conclusion that it could not matter to investors.
Rosa: Correct. Potential material nonpublic information must be handled through the actual controls, not through an improvised materiality judgment.
Dev: If there were a legitimate reason to involve someone from another team, the access process would need to be followed first.
Rosa: Yes. Any wall-crossing must follow the firm's requirements and applicable law, including the consequences for the person's activities.
Dev: I also should not reveal whether the company appears on a confidential monitoring or restriction list.
Rosa: Correct. A restricted list or monitoring status can carry sensitive information; follow the actual handling rules.
Dev: I will tell the colleague I cannot confirm confidential matters and that their question needs the designated compliance route.
Rosa: Good. Their public-side research should remain based on information permitted for that role and its applicable restrictions.
Dev: If material is accidentally sent across the boundary, I will report it promptly rather than forward it or erase the history.
Rosa: Follow the actual record preservation and access instructions. A clear boundary and timely escalation protect the client and both teams without requiring you to make an unauthorized legal decision.
Vocabulary in this exchange: material nonpublic information: Nonpublic information meeting the relevant materiality standard. / information barrier: Controls separating access and communication between activities. / need-to-know access: Access limited to a legitimate authorized purpose. / wall-crossing: Controlled process for bringing someone inside an information boundary under actual rules. / restricted list: Controlled list used for specified compliance restrictions. / client confidentiality: Duty or obligation to protect relevant client information.
END REFERENCE

Lesson 01: Clarifying an institutional investment mandate
Original fictional case: Foundation trustee Nora describes a five-year growth objective for a portfolio. The foundation also needs USD 2 million for a committed payment in six months. Trustee willingness to accept market volatility does not remove that cash requirement. Portfolio manager David is clarifying the mandate; no asset allocation, product selection, or trading authorization has been approved.
Language workshop: A five-year objective includes a six-month cash need
Communication goal: Separate investment objectives, liquidity requirements, and authority before discussing an allocation.
Language guidance: A five-year objective does not give every dollar a five-year horizon. The committed six-month payment must remain visible in the mandate discussion.
Useful expressions (preserve the supplied facts): The growth objective and the committed payment have different time horizons. / How much must be available, in which currency, and by what date? / Willingness to accept volatility is not the same as capacity to miss the payment. / Which body can approve the mandate and any changes? / That is an objective, not an assured return. / The six-month payment needs to remain explicit in the instructions. / We need the full cash-flow schedule before assessing the proposal. / We have clarified requirements, not approved an allocation or trade. / Are you asking about the finding or the next step? / Please correct me if I have misunderstood that detail. / That is what the current record says; it has not been independently confirmed. / That is a possibility, not an agreed outcome. / That decision sits outside my authority. / Who is responsible for that specific next step? / Let me restate the distinction more clearly. / We agree on the action, the owner, and the point for review.
Vocabulary: investment mandate: Agreed objectives, constraints, and authority for investment management. / investment policy statement: Document setting out investment objectives, constraints, and governance. / investment objective: Financial aim the investment strategy is intended to pursue. / time horizon: Period relevant to an investment goal or obligation. / liquidity requirement: Need for funds to be available at specified times. / risk tolerance: Willingness and ability to bear investment risk in the relevant context. / risk capacity: Financial ability to withstand loss or illiquidity. / return objective: Target outcome subject to risk and assumptions, not a guarantee. / capital preservation: Objective of protecting capital under the stated strategy and risks. / spending policy: Rules governing distributions or expenditure from assets. / investment constraint: Limit affecting permissible investment decisions. / restricted asset: Holding subject to a relevant legal, contractual, or policy limitation. / discretionary authority: Authorized power to make specified decisions without separate approval each time. / client governing body: Body authorized to make decisions for the institutional client. / mandate amendment: Authorized change to the agreed investment instructions. / cash-flow schedule: Timetable of expected or committed cash movements. / liability matching: Relating assets or cash flows to specified obligations. / suitability assessment: Evaluation against the relevant client circumstances and applicable requirements. / clarification request: Question that resolves an unclear meaning or instruction. / source attribution: Identification of where information came from. / working assumption: Provisional premise used while information is incomplete. / scope boundary: Limit of the work or authority being discussed. / action owner: Named person responsible for a specified next step. / check-back: Restatement used to verify that a message was understood.
Speaking task: Read the corrected intake and distinguish willingness, capacity, liquidity, and authority. Switch roles and state the two supplied horizons and the exact payment amount without selecting an investment. Complete the four-line follow-up with the supplied choices. Check the explanations, then read the corrected exchange twice, changing roles.
Partner: Nora: Foundation trustee / David: Portfolio manager
Guided response task: Select supplied answers for the dialogue gaps. Check the explanations, then read the completed exchange aloud; no original writing is required.
Optional second-round challenge: A trustee suggests a revised return target in an email. The governing board has not approved a mandate amendment.
Model for comparison AFTER my attempt, not a response to give me first: Nora: The policy document should bring the objective, cash need, restrictions, and governance together in one place.
David: That is the role of the investment policy statement, using the actual agreed instructions and keeping unresolved items visible.
Nora: I will return with the complete schedule and board requirements before we review any proposed allocation.
David: Then we can complete the appropriate suitability assessment and mandate process. We have clarified the questions, not selected a product, guaranteed a return, or authorized a trade.
END REFERENCE
